title: Karpov's squeeze
summary: Nice, 1974: Anatoly Karpov takes away every useful move from his opponent until he gives up with equal material.

steps.title: Nice, 1974
steps.text: Anatoly Karpov became world champion in 1975, when Bobby Fischer did not defend his title, and then held it for ten years. His style was a slow squeeze: grab space, take away the opponent's good squares, and wait. At the 1974 Olympiad in Nice he played the West German grandmaster Wolfgang Unzicker.
steps.narration: Nice, 1974. A young Anatoly Karpov, soon to be world champion, against Wolfgang Unzicker. Watch a squeeze.

steps.title: Karpov – Unzicker, Nice Olympiad 1974
steps.text: A closed Ruy Lopez. Nothing dramatic happens for a long time: Karpov locks the center, takes the a-file, and slowly pushes Black's pieces back until they have nothing to do.
steps.narration: No fireworks here. Karpov takes squares, files and space, one quiet move at a time.

notes.text: 13.d5: Karpov closes the center. Now the fight moves to the wings.
15.axb5: the a-file opens. Karpov wants it for his rooks.
22...c4: Unzicker closes the queenside too. His pieces are getting short of room.
24.Ba7!: a surprising square. The bishop sits deep in Black's camp where no pawn can chase it, and Black's rook on a8 has no file.
26.Rea1: both white rooks on the a-file.
30.f4: with the queenside locked, Karpov opens a second front on the kingside.
31.f5: the kingside is locked as well. White has more space everywhere.
41.Bxf7+: the light-square bishops come off. Now g6 is a hole.
44.Nh5: material is exactly equal, yet Unzicker resigned. His pieces are stuck, and White's queen and knights are closing in on the king.

guesses.prompt: Karpov wants to trade off Black's best defender of the light squares.
guesses.hint: Your light-square bishop can offer a trade to the bishop on f7.
guesses.why: 35.Bh5 offers a trade of light-square bishops. Once they are gone, g6 and f7 near Black's king become holes.

guesses.prompt: The bishops are gone. Where does the queen go?
guesses.hint: Use the square the bishop just left.
guesses.why: 42.Qh5 aims at g6, the hole in front of the king. Next comes Qg6 and a knight to h5.

guesses.prompt: The queen is on h5. Move her into the hole.
guesses.hint: Which square in front of Black's king can no black pawn ever cover again?
guesses.why: 43.Qg6 plants the queen next to the black king. No pawn can chase her, and the knights are coming to help.

steps.title: Why resign?
steps.question: At the end, material was exactly equal. Why did Unzicker resign?

options.text: His pieces had no good moves and could not stop White's threats
options.why: Right. Karpov took away every useful square, so material did not matter.
Nothing in the game shows that. The position itself was lost.

options.text: He had a forced checkmate against him in one move
options.why: There was no mate in one. The threats came slowly, but they could not be stopped.

steps.narration: Material was equal. Why did Black give up?

steps.title: Take away the good moves
steps.text: Karpov won without a single sacrifice. He grabbed space, put a bishop where it could never be chased, owned the a-file, and traded off the pieces that defended Black's weak squares. When your opponent has no useful moves, the position can be lost even with equal material.
steps.narration: You do not always need to win material. Take away your opponent's good moves, and the position wins itself.
